unit.unitOverview: This unit is about the documents and conversations that decide whether you get work. Level 1 Unit 11 gave you the language of describing a job; this one gives you the language of applying for one — the suffixes that name professions, the compressed register of a CV, and the structure that turns an interview answer from a claim into evidence. It ends with the same answer given twice, once as an assertion and once with evidence.

Do the Practice. Practice 3 is the diagnostic — claim or evidence.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about applying for work, and it has one idea in it that matters more than all the vocabulary.
First pattern: the suffixes that name professions.
English builds most job titles from a verb or a noun plus one of four endings, and knowing which is which lets you produce a job title you have never been taught.
-er and -or both mean the person who does the thing. Teach becomes teacher. Drive becomes driver. Supervise becomes supervisor. Inspect becomes inspector.
There is no rule that tells you which of the two a given word takes, and I want to be straightforward about that — it is a spelling fact learned with each word. But there is a weak tendency worth having: -or attaches more often to Latin-origin verbs ending in -ate, -it or -ct. Operate, operator. Inspect, inspector. Edit, editor. Supervise is an exception and it is a common one.
-ist means somebody who practises a specialism or holds a belief. Special becomes specialist. Science becomes scientist. Art becomes artist. Analyse becomes analyst — and notice that one drops a syllable.
-ian usually attaches to a field and means a person qualified in it. Electricity becomes electrician. Technic becomes technician. Music becomes musician. And notice the stress moves: ELECtric but elecTRICian. That is a general pattern with -ian and it catches people out when they say the word for the first time.
There are two more worth having. -ant and -ent, from Latin: consultant, assistant, accountant, superintendent. And -ee, which is the opposite of -er — it names the person the action is done to. Employer and employee. Interviewer and interviewee. Trainer and trainee. That pair is worth knowing because it is completely regular and it is one of the few places where English gives you a genuine rule.
Second pattern: the register of a CV.
A CV is not written in ordinary English. It has its own compressed grammar and it is worth learning explicitly, because writing one in normal sentences makes it read as amateurish for reasons that have nothing to do with your English.
The rules are these.
No I. A CV never says I managed a team. It says Managed a team of six. The subject is dropped entirely, and it is understood.
Start with a verb, in the past tense for previous roles and the present for the current one. Managed. Coordinated. Implemented. Reduced.
No articles where you can drop them. Managed team of six, or managed a team of six — both appear, and the shorter is more usual.
Numbers wherever possible. Managed a team of six is stronger than managed a small team. Reduced processing time by 40 per cent is stronger than improved efficiency.
And the verb should be the strongest accurate one. Coordinated is stronger than helped with. Implemented is stronger than was involved in. But it must be accurate — if you coordinated nothing, coordinated is a lie, and it is the kind that unravels in an interview.
A covering letter is the opposite register. It is written in full sentences, in the first person, and its job is to say what the CV cannot: why these particular things add up to this particular application.
So the two documents are not two versions of the same thing. The CV is a compressed record. The letter is the argument.
Third pattern, and this is the one that matters.
An interview question is almost always a request for evidence, and almost everybody answers it with a claim.
The question: are you good at working under pressure?
The claim answer: yes, I work well under pressure. I stay calm and I prioritise.
That answer is true, fluent, grammatically perfect, and completely useless, because everybody says it. The interviewer has heard it eleven times that day and it does not distinguish you from anybody.
The evidence answer has a shape, and once you know the shape you can produce it for any question.
Situation. Task. Action. Result.
What was happening. What you had to do. What you actually did. What happened as a result.
Last December we lost two of four drivers in the same week — that is the situation. I had to keep the deliveries running with half the fleet — that is the task. I rebuilt the routes so each remaining driver covered two zones instead of one, and I moved the two least urgent contracts to the following week after ringing both customers — that is the action. We missed one delivery out of about ninety, and both customers stayed — that is the result.
That is one story and it took forty seconds, and it demonstrates working under pressure without ever using the phrase.
The key move is the last one. Give the result, with a number if you have one. Most people stop after the action, and the action alone leaves the interviewer to work out whether it succeeded.
And here is the thing that makes this genuinely useful rather than a technique. You need about six of these stories, prepared, from your actual working life. Six stories will answer almost any competency question, because interview questions repeat: pressure, conflict, a mistake, a change, working with somebody difficult, something you improved.
Preparing six stories is a manageable evening's work. Preparing an answer to every possible question is not.
One more thing about the difficult questions. Tell me about a mistake you made. The answer is a real mistake, stated plainly, with what you did about it and what you changed afterwards. The result section is what turns it from a confession into evidence. An answer that avoids naming a mistake fails the question, and everybody in the room knows it.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Naming the Person Who Does It
readings.passageScript:
Most English job titles are built from a verb or a field plus one of a small number of endings, and knowing them lets you produce a title you have never been taught.
-er and -or both mean the person who does the thing.
Teach, teacher. Drive, driver. Manage, manager.
Supervise, supervisor. Inspect, inspector. Operate, operator.
There is no rule for which of the two a word takes. It is a spelling fact learned with each word, and there is one weak tendency: -or attaches more often to Latin-origin verbs ending in -ate, -it and -ct. Operator, editor, inspector, director. Supervisor is a common exception to its own pattern.
-ist names somebody who practises a specialism or holds a belief.
Special, specialist. Science, scientist. Art, artist. Analyse, analyst — and note that one loses a syllable.
-ian usually attaches to a field and names a person qualified in it.
Electricity, electrician. Music, musician. Technic, technician. Library, librarian.
And here is the practical point about -ian, because it catches people the first time they say one of these words aloud. The stress moves to the syllable immediately before the ending.
ELECtric becomes elecTRICian.
TECHnical becomes techNICian.
MUsic becomes muSICian.
Getting the stress wrong is more noticeable than getting a vowel wrong, and it is entirely predictable with this ending.
Two more are worth having.
-ant and -ent, from Latin: consultant, assistant, accountant, superintendent.
And -ee, which is the reverse of -er. It names the person the action is done to, and it is one of the few genuinely regular patterns in English word-building.
Employer and employee. Interviewer and interviewee. Trainer and trainee. Payer and payee. Referrer and referee.
In every pair the -er does the thing and the -ee receives it, without exception.

readings.title: A CV Is Not Written in English
readings.passageScript:
A CV has its own grammar, and writing one in ordinary sentences makes it read as amateurish for reasons that have nothing to do with the quality of your English.
The rules are few and they are strict.
No I. Ever. A CV does not say I managed a team of six. It says Managed a team of six. The subject is dropped and understood, and a CV that says I in every line looks wrong to anybody who reads them regularly.
Start with a verb. Past tense for previous roles, present for the current one. Managed. Coordinated. Implemented. Negotiated. Reduced.
Drop what can be dropped. Managed a team of six, or managed team of six — both appear and the shorter is more usual in bullet points.
Use numbers wherever you honestly can. This is the single biggest improvement most CVs need.
Managed a small team becomes managed a team of six.
Improved efficiency becomes reduced processing time from twenty minutes to eight.
Dealt with customers becomes handled about forty enquiries a day.
The number does two things. It makes the claim checkable, and it tells the reader the scale you have operated at, which is usually what they are actually trying to find out.
Choose the strongest accurate verb. Coordinated is stronger than helped with. Implemented is stronger than was involved in. Negotiated is stronger than discussed.
But accurate is doing real work in that sentence. If you did not coordinate anything, coordinated is a lie, and it is the kind that comes apart in an interview when somebody asks you to describe how you did it.
A covering letter is the opposite register in almost every respect. Full sentences. First person. Connected argument.
Its job is the one thing the CV structurally cannot do: explain why these particular experiences add up to this particular application.
So the two documents are not long and short versions of each other. The CV is a compressed record of what happened. The letter is the argument about what it means.

readings.title: The Claim and the Evidence
readings.setting: The same candidate answering the same question, in a practice session and then in the interview.
readings.passageScript:
QUESTION
  "Can you tell me about a time you had to
   work under pressure?"

-----------------------------------------

  ANSWER A - the practice session

  Yes, I work well under pressure. I think
  the main thing is staying calm and
  prioritising properly. In my current
  role there's a lot of pressure,
  especially at busy times, and I've
  always been able to handle it. I'm quite
  organised and I don't panic. I think
  that's one of my strengths.

-----------------------------------------

  ANSWER B - what she said in the
  interview

  Last December we lost two of our four
  drivers in the same week - one left and
  one was signed off.

  I had to keep about ninety deliveries a
  week running with half the fleet, over
  the busiest fortnight of the year.

  I rebuilt the routes so each remaining
  driver covered two zones instead of one,
  which meant longer days but no gaps. Then
  I rang the two least urgent customers and
  asked whether they'd take delivery the
  following week. Both agreed.

  We missed one delivery out of about
  ninety, and we kept both customers. The
  route change is still in use.

grammar.title: Profession suffixes
grammar.explanation: Job titles are built from a verb or a field plus one of a small set of endings. Most of it has to be learned, but two parts of it are completely predictable.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
-ER and -OR = the person who DOES it
  teach -> teacher   drive -> driver
  supervise -> supervisor
  inspect -> inspector
  operate -> operator

  NO RULE for which. Learned with the word.
  weak tendency: -OR after Latin verbs
  ending -ate, -it, -ct
     operator, editor, inspector, director

-IST = practises a specialism
  special -> specialist
  science -> scientist
  analyse -> analyst  (drops a syllable)

-IAN = qualified in a field
  electricity -> electrician
  technic -> technician
  music -> musician

  THE STRESS MOVES - predictable
     ELECtric  -> elecTRICian
     TECHnical -> techNICian
     MUsic     -> muSICian

-ANT / -ENT
  consultant, assistant, accountant

-EE = the person it is DONE TO
  employer / employee
  interviewer / interviewee
  trainer / trainee
  ^ completely regular. No exceptions.
grammar.workedExample:
You want the word for somebody qualified to work with electricity.
1. The base is a field rather than a verb, so -ian is likely.
2. Electricity becomes electrician.
3. Now the stress. With -ian it moves to the syllable immediately before the ending.
4. So it is elecTRICian, not ELECtrician.
5. Compare the adjective: elecTRIC. The stress is already there, and the -ian keeps it in the same relative place.
Now one where you have to guess. You want the person who operates something.
1. It is a verb, so -er or -or.
2. Operate ends in -ate, and the tendency says Latin verbs ending in -ate take -or.
3. Result: operator. The tendency held.
And one that is completely reliable. Somebody is being trained.
1. The person doing the training takes -er: trainer.
2. The person receiving it takes -ee: trainee.
That pair never fails.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting the stress on the wrong syllable in -ian words — ELECtrician, TECHnician. It is more noticeable to a listener than a wrong vowel and it is entirely predictable. The other error is inventing -er where -or belongs, or the reverse; there is no rule, so a word you are unsure about should be checked rather than guessed at in writing.
grammar.memoryTip: -ee receives, -er does. With -ian, the stress moves just before the ending.
grammar.practice:
Build the word for the person, and mark the stressed syllable in any -ian word.
1. teach
2. supervise
3. operate
4. electricity
5. technic
6. music
7. analyse
8. consult
9. somebody who is employed
10. somebody who is interviewed
11. somebody who is trained
12. science
grammar.answerKey:
1. teacher  2. supervisor  3. operator  4. elecTRICian  5. techNICian  6. muSICian  7. analyst  8. consultant  9. employee  10. interviewee  11. trainee  12. scientist
Numbers 4, 5 and 6 all move the stress to the syllable before -ian, without exception.
Numbers 9, 10 and 11 all take -ee because the person receives the action. Their -er partners are employer, interviewer and trainer.
Numbers 2 and 3 both take -or, and only 3 follows the tendency — operate ends in -ate. Supervise does not, and it takes -or anyway, which is why the tendency is a guess rather than a rule.

grammar.title: The register of a CV
grammar.explanation: A CV has its own compressed grammar. Writing one in ordinary sentences makes it read as amateurish for reasons unconnected to the quality of your English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
NO I. EVER.
  I managed a team of six.     X
  Managed a team of six.       right

START WITH A VERB
  past for previous roles
  present for the current one
     Managed. Coordinated.
     Implemented. Negotiated.

USE NUMBERS WHEREVER HONEST
  managed a small team
     -> managed a team of six
  improved efficiency
     -> reduced processing time from
        twenty minutes to eight

  a number makes it CHECKABLE and shows
  the SCALE you have worked at.

STRONGEST ACCURATE VERB
  helped with     -> coordinated
  was involved in -> implemented
  discussed       -> negotiated

  ACCURATE is doing real work here.
  A verb you cannot back up comes apart
  in the interview.

THE COVERING LETTER IS THE OPPOSITE
  full sentences, first person, argument.
  It says why these things add up to
  THIS application. The CV cannot.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to put on your CV that you were responsible for a small team.
1. Drop the subject. No I.
2. Start with a verb in the past tense: Managed.
3. Now add a number, because managed a small team tells the reader nothing about scale.
4. Result: Managed a team of six across two shifts.
Now one where the verb needs strengthening.
1. You want to say you were part of introducing a new system.
2. Was involved in the new system is weak and vague.
3. What did you actually do? You wrote the training and ran the changeover for one site.
4. Choose the strongest accurate verb for that: Implemented the new stock system at one site, including training twelve staff.
5. Check the honesty constraint. Did you implement it? At one site, yes — and the sentence says so. Implemented the new stock system with no qualifier would be a claim you could not defend.
The number and the qualifier together are what make it both stronger and safer.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing a CV in full sentences with I, which is grammatically perfect and immediately marks the document as inexperienced. The other error is the opposite of vagueness: choosing a verb stronger than the facts support, which reads well on paper and collapses the moment somebody asks you to describe how you did it.
grammar.memoryTip: No I, verb first, a number wherever you honestly can.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each in CV register.
1. I was responsible for a small team.
2. I helped with the new stock system.
3. I dealt with customers every day.
4. I improved efficiency in the booking-in process.
5. I talked to two suppliers about their prices.
6. I was involved in training new staff.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Managed a team of six across two shifts.
2. Implemented the new stock system at one site, including training twelve staff.
3. Handled about forty customer enquiries a day.
4. Streamlined the booking-in process, reducing it from twenty minutes to eight.
5. Negotiated new terms with two suppliers, reducing unit cost by a fifth.
6. Trained eleven new staff over eighteen months.
Every version drops I and starts with a past-tense verb.
Every version adds a number. That is the change that does most of the work — six, twelve, forty, twenty to eight, a fifth, eleven.
Every verb is stronger than the original: managed, implemented, handled, streamlined, negotiated, trained. Each is defensible if the numbers are true, and none of them is defensible if they are not.

grammar.title: Answering with evidence
grammar.explanation: An interview question is a request for evidence, and almost everybody answers it with a claim. This card gives the shape that turns one into the other.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE QUESTION ASKS FOR EVIDENCE

  "Are you good at working under pressure?"

  CLAIM ANSWER
     "Yes, I stay calm and prioritise."
     true, fluent, and useless -
     everybody says it.

  EVIDENCE ANSWER - four parts

  SITUATION  what was happening
  TASK       what you had to do
  ACTION     what you actually did
  RESULT     what happened, with a number

MOST PEOPLE STOP AFTER THE ACTION.
  The result is what proves it worked.

PREPARE SIX STORIES, NOT ANSWERS
  questions repeat: pressure, conflict,
  a mistake, a change, a difficult
  person, something you improved.

THE STRONGEST ANSWER NEVER NAMES
THE QUALITY. It demonstrates it.

THE MISTAKE QUESTION
  name a real one, plainly. Say what you
  did and what you changed. The RESULT
  turns a confession into evidence.
grammar.workedExample:
You are asked whether you work well under pressure.
1. Resist answering the question directly. Yes, I do is a claim and everybody gives it.
2. Find a real story. Last December, two of four drivers gone in one week.
3. Situation: state it in one sentence, with the numbers. We lost two of our four drivers in the same week.
4. Task: what you had to achieve. I had to keep about ninety deliveries a week running with half the fleet, over the busiest fortnight of the year.
5. Action: what you actually did, specifically. I rebuilt the routes so each driver covered two zones, and I rang the two least urgent customers to ask whether they would take delivery the following week.
6. Result: what happened, with a number. We missed one delivery out of about ninety and kept both customers.
7. Add what survived, if anything did: the route change is still in use.
Forty seconds, and the phrase under pressure never appears. The interviewer draws the conclusion, which is far more convincing than being told it.
grammar.commonMistake: Stopping after the action. It is the commonest fault in interview answers and it leaves the listener to work out whether what you did succeeded — which they will not do generously. The other error is answering the mistake question by avoiding a mistake: a candidate who cannot name one has failed the question, and everybody in the room knows it.
grammar.memoryTip: Situation, task, action, result. Never stop before the result.
grammar.practice:
Take four questions and plan an answer for each in four parts. One line per part.
1. Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.
2. Tell me about a disagreement with a colleague.
3. Tell me about a mistake you made.
4. Tell me about something you improved.
grammar.answerKey:
Model for question 3, the hardest one:
Situation: I sent a price list to a customer that had not been updated after the March increase.
Task: They had already placed an order at the old prices, and I had to sort it out before it was invoiced.
Action: I rang them the same morning, explained it was my error, and asked whether they wanted to keep the order at the correct price or cancel. They kept it. Then I asked for the shared price file to be date-stamped so the current version is obvious.
Result: We kept the order and the customer, we lost about eighty pounds on that one job, and nobody has sent an out-of-date list since the file was changed.
Check yours against three things. Is the situation specific enough to be real? Does the action say what you personally did, rather than what the team did? And is there a result with a number or a clear outcome in it?
For question 3 specifically: a real mistake, plainly named. An answer that avoids naming one has not answered the question.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A CV section and a covering paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Take one role you have held — a job, a placement, a volunteer position, a substantial responsibility.
Write it twice.
Part A: six CV bullet points. No I, verb first, a number in at least four of them, and the strongest accurate verb in each.
Part B: one covering-letter paragraph in full sentences and the first person, saying why those six things add up to a reason to consider you for something specific.
Then write two lines: which bullet point you were tempted to overstate, and what the letter says that the bullets cannot.
writing.modelText:
PART A — Warehouse Supervisor, Meridian Freight, 2019 to present
· Manage a team of six across two shifts.
· Coordinate inbound deliveries from four suppliers, averaging ninety a week.
· Streamlined the booking-in process, reducing it from twenty minutes to eight.
· Trained eleven new staff over eighteen months; nine are still in post.
· Negotiated revised terms with two suppliers, cutting unit cost by a fifth.
· Rebuilt delivery routing during a staffing shortage; the change is still in use.

PART B
I have spent nine years in warehouse operations and the last five running a bay, and what I have found I am actually good at is not the day-to-day supervision but the point where a process is not working and nobody has time to look at it. The booking-in change and the routing rebuild both came out of that, and both are still in place, which matters more to me than the savings. I am applying for this role because it is the first one I have seen that is explicitly about process rather than about headcount, and I would rather do that deliberately than keep doing it in the gaps.

1. I was tempted to write negotiated terms with suppliers without saying two. Two is a small number and it is the true one, and a reader who assumed six would find out in the interview.
2. The letter says why the six things belong together. The bullets show that I improved two processes; only the letter says that this is the part of the job I am best at and the reason I am applying.
writing.expectedLength: Six bullet points plus one paragraph
writing.successCriteria: Six bullets with no I, each starting with a verb, at least four containing a number, each using the strongest accurate verb; one covering paragraph in full first-person sentences making an argument the bullets cannot; two lines identifying a temptation to overstate and what the letter adds
writing.support: Write the numbers first, on their own line — how many people, how many deliveries, how much time, how many trained. Then build a bullet around each. Starting from the verb produces vague bullets; starting from the number does not.
writing.extension: Give Part A to somebody and ask them to guess the size of the operation you work in. If they are far out, the numbers are not doing their job.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Six stories
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write six interview stories from your own working, studying or volunteering life.
Each in four parts, one or two sentences per part: situation, task, action, result.
The six must cover: pressure, a disagreement, a mistake, a change you had to adapt to, a difficult person, and something you improved.
Each result must contain a number or a clear outcome.
Then write two lines: which story was hardest to write, and which of the six you would use if you were only allowed one.
writing.modelText:
STORY 3 — a mistake
Situation: In March I sent a customer a price list that had not been updated after the annual increase.
Task: They placed an order at the old prices, and I had to resolve it before it was invoiced.
Action: I rang them the same morning, told them it was my error, and offered them the choice of keeping the order at the correct price or cancelling it. They kept it. I then asked for the shared price file to be date-stamped so that the current version is obvious at a glance.
Result: We kept the order and the customer, we absorbed about eighty pounds on that job, and nobody has sent an out-of-date list in the fourteen months since the file was changed.

1. The mistake story was hardest, and not for the reason I expected — naming the mistake was fine, and finding a result I could evidence was the difficult part.
2. I would use the pressure story, because it has the clearest numbers in it and because the change I made is still in use, which the others cannot say.
writing.expectedLength: Six stories in four parts each
writing.successCriteria: Six stories covering the six required areas; four labelled parts in each; every action says what the writer personally did; every result contains a number or a clear outcome; the mistake story names a real mistake plainly; two lines of reflection
writing.support: Write the results first for all six. If you cannot state a result, the story is probably not one you should use, and it is better to find that out now than in the room.
writing.extension: Time yourself saying each one aloud. Anything over about a minute needs the situation shortening — that is almost always where the excess is.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two answers
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the two answers in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Answer A is fluent, true and grammatically perfect. Why does it fail?
2. Identify the four parts of Answer B and say which sentences form each.
3. Answer B never says the words under pressure. Does that weaken it? Explain.
4. What does the final sentence of B add, and why does it matter?
5. Rewrite Answer A as an evidence answer, inventing plausible detail.
writing.modelText:
1. Because it is a claim rather than evidence. Nothing in it could be checked, and every candidate says a version of it, so it gives the interviewer no way to distinguish this person from the others they have seen that day.
2. Situation: the first paragraph — losing two of four drivers in one week. Task: the second — keeping ninety deliveries a week running with half the fleet over the busiest fortnight. Action: the third — rebuilding the routes into two zones per driver, and ringing the two least urgent customers. Result: the fourth — one missed delivery out of ninety, both customers retained, and the route change still in use.
3. No, it strengthens it. Naming the quality asks the interviewer to accept a description; demonstrating it lets them reach the conclusion themselves, which is far more convincing. The question was a request for evidence and B supplies it.
4. It says the route change is still in use, which shows the solution was durable rather than an emergency measure abandoned afterwards. It turns coping with a crisis into a lasting improvement, and most candidates stop before saying anything of the kind.
5. Model: Two weeks before Christmas we had four large orders due on the same day and one van off the road. I had to get all four out without telling any of the customers we were short. I split the deliveries across two days, rang the two customers whose contracts allowed a day's flexibility, and did the last run myself after my shift. All four orders arrived within the agreed window, and we have kept the two-day split for December ever since.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 maps all four parts to specific sentences; answer 3 argues that not naming the quality strengthens the answer; answer 5 supplies all four parts with at least one number
writing.support: Count the checkable facts in each answer. Answer A has none. Answer B has at least six — four drivers, two lost, ninety deliveries, one missed, two customers, one fortnight. That count is most of the answer to question 1.
writing.extension: Write the follow-up question an interviewer would ask after Answer A, and after Answer B. Only one of them has anything to ask about.
